0.title: One God in Three Persons
0.essay:
Christians believe in one God who exists eternally as three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Each is fully God, yet there are not three gods but one. The word “Trinity” is not in the Bible, but the truth it names is on almost every page of the New Testament.

Not a footnote

Many believers find the Trinity confusing and quietly avoid it, thinking of it as a puzzle for theologians with little to do with everyday faith. Yet the Trinity is not a footnote to Christianity. It is the shape of the God we worship. Every Christian prayer is offered to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit. Every Christian is baptised in the one name “of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). Salvation itself is the work of the three persons together.

We will never fully comprehend the Trinity; we are creatures speaking of our Creator. But we can know what Scripture says, avoid the errors that distort it, and grow in love for the God who has revealed himself as Father, Son and Spirit.

The chapters

One God lays the foundation: Christianity is not belief in many gods. Three Persons shows from Scripture that Father, Son and Spirit are each fully God and distinct from one another. The Trinity Revealed traces how God made this known in history. Guarding the Truth names the errors the church has had to resist. The Trinity and Our Salvation shows how all three persons save us. And Living with the Triune God explores how this truth shapes prayer, worship, love and hope. This study belongs alongside the Attributes of God and the studies on Christ and the Holy Spirit.

1.title: One God
1.essay:
The foundation of the doctrine of the Trinity is that there is only one God. Christianity is not polytheism. Before we can speak rightly of Father, Son and Spirit, we must hear the confession that shaped Israel and the first Christians: the LORD is one.

Israel’s confession

“Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:4–5). Israel was to speak these words lying down and rising up. In a world crowded with gods, Israel worshipped one. Because the LORD is one, he must be loved with the whole person; there is no other god to share a divided heart with.

Through Isaiah, God spoke even to Cyrus, a pagan king he would use to free his people: “I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God” (Isaiah 45:5). He forms light and creates darkness; everything comes from the one LORD, so that people from east to west may know there is none besides him.

The New Testament agrees

When a scribe asked which commandment was most important, Jesus answered with the Shema: “Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Mark 12:29). The Son of God himself confesses that God is one. James writes, “You believe that God is one; you do well” (James 2:19). The first Christians were Jews who never stopped believing in one God.

And then Paul says something remarkable. Writing about food offered to idols, he insists that “there is no God but one” — and continues, “yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist” (1 Corinthians 8:4–6). He takes the words of the Shema — “God” and “Lord” — and places Jesus inside the confession of the one God. The one God is Father and Son.

One being, not a committee

The Father, Son and Spirit are not three gods working together like partners in a business. They share one divine being, one will and one power. Whatever God does, the three persons do together. When Christians say God is one, they mean there is one divine nature. The three persons do not each have a third of God; each is the whole God. That is a mystery beyond our full understanding, but not a contradiction: God is one in one sense (being) and three in another (persons).

Why it matters

If there were many gods, the world would have no single source, no single standard of truth and no single object of worship. The oneness of God means that all of life belongs to him, and that he alone deserves our whole heart. And because God is one, there is no rival power equal to him. Satan is a creature, not an evil god.

Muslims and Jehovah’s Witnesses sometimes say that the Trinity is belief in three gods. Christians reply that the doctrine of the Trinity is the safeguard of belief in one God, not its denial, because it insists that the Son and the Spirit share the one being of God, rather than being lesser gods beside him.

On Mount Carmel, the prophets of Baal cried out all day and no one answered. Elijah prayed once, and fire fell. The people shouted, “The LORD, he is God; the LORD, he is God” (1 Kings 18:39). There is one God, and he answers.

A Christian woman whose Muslim colleague said Christians believe in three gods explained that Christians recite the same confession as Moses: the LORD is one. Then she opened John’s Gospel and showed how Jesus spoke of the Father, himself and the Spirit. They agreed to keep talking.

For reflection

Why is it important that Christians believe in one God, not three? How does 1 Corinthians 8:6 include Jesus in the confession of the one God? If someone asked whether Christians believe in three gods, how would you answer?

2.title: Three Persons
2.essay:
Alongside the oneness of God, the New Testament shows that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are each fully God, and that they are distinct from one another — not one person wearing three masks, but three persons in real relationship.

The Father is God

This is assumed everywhere. Jesus prays to his Father as “the only true God” (John 17:3). Paul begins his letters with grace “from God our Father” (Romans 1:7).

The Son is God

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him” (John 1:1–3). The Word was with God, so he is distinct from the Father. The Word was God, so he shares the Father’s nature. And all things were made through him, so he is not part of creation. In three short verses John lays the foundation of the doctrine of the Trinity.

Thomas confessed the risen Jesus as “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). Paul says that in Christ “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9). And the Father himself says of the Son, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever” (Hebrews 1:8); Hebrews goes on to say that the Son laid the foundation of the earth and will remain when heaven and earth wear out like a garment (Hebrews 1:10–12). The Son creates, forgives sins, receives worship and will judge the world — all things only God can do.

The Spirit is God

When Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit, Peter said he had lied to God (Acts 5:3–4). The Spirit knows the depths of God (1 Corinthians 2:10–11), is present everywhere (Psalm 139:7) and gives life. And he is a person, not a force: he teaches, speaks, intercedes and can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30).

Three, and distinct

The Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Spirit, and the Spirit is not the Father. The Son prays to the Father (John 17). The Father sends the Son (John 3:17). The Spirit speaks not on his own authority but declares what is the Son’s (John 16:13–14). In one sentence Jesus names all three: “when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me” (John 15:26). The three are distinct, yet they act together in perfect harmony.

In the upper room, Jesus said, “the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things” (John 14:26). The Father sends; the Spirit comes in the Son’s name; the Spirit teaches. Three persons, one saving purpose.

One name

The risen Christ sent his disciples to baptise “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). One name, not three names: one God, three persons. Baptism places believers under the name of the triune God. From the first day of the Christian life, the Trinity is the God we belong to.

What “person” means

In this doctrine, a “person” is not a separate being, as three human persons are three separate beings. It means a distinct “who” within the one divine “what”. Our language strains here, because nothing in creation is exactly like God.

The persons are distinguished by their relations. The Father is eternally Father, never without the Son. The Son is eternally begotten of the Father, not made and not created. The Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son. These relations did not begin at creation or at Bethlehem; they are who God eternally is. And the three are equal in power, glory and majesty. The Son is not a lesser god, nor the Spirit a divine energy. Each is to be worshipped.

Praying to the triune God

A Christian man had always prayed to “God” without much thought about whom he was addressing. Studying the Trinity, he began to pray to the Father as a child, to give thanks for the Son by name and to ask for the Spirit’s help. His prayers became warmer and richer. When you pray, do you think of God as Father, Son and Spirit — or as a vague single presence?

For reflection

Which verses most clearly show you that the Son is fully God, and that the Spirit is fully God? How does Scripture show that the three are distinct persons? What does it mean to be baptised into the one “name” of Father, Son and Spirit?

3.title: The Trinity Revealed
3.essay:
The doctrine of the Trinity was not invented by philosophers. God revealed it gradually, in history, and finally in the coming of the Son and the pouring out of the Spirit. We know who God is by what he has done to save us.

Hints in the Old Testament

The Old Testament emphasises God’s oneness, but it contains hints of a richness within God. At creation “the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters”, and God spoke, and there was light (Genesis 1:2–3); John later tells us that the Word through whom God spoke is the Son (John 1:1–3). God says, “Let us make man in our image” (Genesis 1:26). Some explain this as God speaking to angels, or a royal plural; but angels did not create humanity, and the image is God’s alone. In the light of the New Testament, many Christians have seen here a hint of the Trinity.

The angel of the LORD speaks as God and is called God (Genesis 16:13; Exodus 3:2–6). God’s Word and Wisdom act as if personal (Psalm 33:6; Proverbs 8). The coming child is called “Mighty God, Everlasting Father” (Isaiah 9:6). And in the middle of a speech in Isaiah a voice says, “And now the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah 48:16) — the one sent speaking as though he has been with God from the beginning. We should not claim that Old Testament believers fully understood the Trinity. But the New Testament shows the same God at work all along, and invites us to reread the Old with new eyes (Luke 24:27).

Revealed at the Jordan

The full revelation came with Jesus. At his baptism, all three persons appeared together: “And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him; and behold, a voice from heaven said, ‘This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased’” (Matthew 3:16–17). The Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends, the Father speaks — at the very start of Jesus’ public ministry.

Revealed in Jesus’ teaching

Jesus spoke constantly of his Father and promised the Spirit. In John 14–17, the night before his death, he spoke of the three persons more than anywhere else: the Father loves the Son, the Son obeys the Father, the Spirit glorifies the Son. At Pentecost, Peter’s first sermon was Trinitarian without using the word: “Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing” (Acts 2:33).

Revealed in the church’s worship

The early church did not sit down and design a doctrine. They worshipped Jesus as Lord, experienced the Spirit poured out and prayed to the Father. Their letters are full of Trinitarian patterns, often without explanation, because this was simply how they knew God. Peter greets believers who are “elect exiles… according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and for sprinkling with his blood” (1 Peter 1:1–2). Jude urges believers to build themselves up, “praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Jude 20–21).

Revelation in action

Notice how God revealed the Trinity: not mainly by explaining it, but by acting. The Father sent the Son; the Son died and rose; the Spirit was poured out. The doctrine came from the drama of salvation.

A Bible study group reading Genesis 1 discussed the words “Let us make man.” A new believer asked, “So the Trinity was there from the beginning?” The leader turned to John 1:1–3 and Genesis 1:2, and the group saw the Father, the Word and the Spirit together at creation. Next time you read a Gospel, look for places where the Father, Son and Spirit appear together. You will find more than you expect.

For reflection

Which Old Testament hints of the Trinity do you find most striking? Read Matthew 3:13–17: what does each person do? Why do you think God revealed the Trinity gradually rather than all at once?

4.title: Guarding the Truth
4.essay:
Through history, many have tried to make the Trinity simpler by giving up part of what Scripture says. The church has had to guard the truth by naming these errors. Knowing them helps us recognise and avoid them today.

One person in three disguises

Some taught that God is one person who appears in three modes or roles: as Father in creation, as Son in redemption, as Spirit in the church. This is called modalism, and it is still common, often through illustrations like water being ice, liquid and steam. But Scripture shows the three persons existing at the same time and relating to one another. At Jesus’ baptism the Son is in the water, the Spirit descends and the Father speaks. The Son prays to the Father: “glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5). Modalism turns all this into a kind of play-acting.

The Son as a creature

Others taught that the Son is the first and highest creature, but not fully God. This was the teaching of Arius in the fourth century, and Jehovah’s Witnesses teach it today. But Scripture says all things were made through the Son (John 1:3); he cannot be part of creation if he made all of it. He is “the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3). He is not a high angel; he is far above the angels. The great creed of the fourth century confessed the Son as “true God from true God… of one being with the Father”.

Jehovah’s Witnesses appeal to Colossians 1:15, where Christ is called “the firstborn of all creation”. But the next verse says, “by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible” (Colossians 1:16). “Firstborn” here means supreme rank and heir, as Israel was God’s firstborn son (Exodus 4:22) and God made David “the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth” (Psalm 89:27). The Son is Creator, not creature.

When Jesus said, “the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), he spoke as the incarnate Son in his humble role as servant, not of a lesser divine nature. The same Jesus said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). His hearers understood him clearly: they picked up stones, saying, “you, being a man, make yourself God” (John 10:33). Jesus did not correct them by saying he was a lesser being.

Three gods

Others go the opposite way, treating the Father, Son and Spirit as three separate gods who simply agree with each other. This is tritheism, and it denies the oneness of God that Scripture insists on.

A word about illustrations

Every illustration of the Trinity fails somewhere. An egg — shell, white and yolk — makes each person a part of God. Water as ice, liquid and steam suggests modalism. A man who is a father, a son and a husband is one person in three roles. It is wiser to say that God is unique, and to stay close to the words of Scripture.

A youth leader who had always explained the Trinity with the water illustration changed his approach after learning about modalism. “God is unlike anything else,” he told his group. “Let’s look at what the Bible says about the Father, the Son and the Spirit.” The young people found the Bible’s own words more convincing than the illustration.

Why the creeds matter

The early creeds did not add to Scripture. They summarised it and fenced it against error. When believers today confess the Trinity — perhaps in the words of the Nicene or Apostles’ Creed — they stand with the church through the ages, guarding the truth that Christ is fully God, the Spirit is fully God, and God is one.

For reflection

What is modalism, and why is it wrong? How would you answer someone who says Colossians 1:15 shows Jesus was created? Which illustration of the Trinity have you used, and what does it get wrong?

5.title: The Trinity and Our Salvation
5.essay:
The Trinity is not only a truth about God in himself. It is the shape of our salvation. Every part of it is the work of the Father, the Son and the Spirit together.

The Father plans, the Son accomplishes, the Spirit applies

Ephesians 1:3–14 is a single long sentence in Paul’s Greek — a hymn of praise to the triune God. The Father chose us: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:3–4). The Son redeemed us: “In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses” (Ephesians 1:7). The Spirit sealed us: “In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance” (Ephesians 1:13–14). Each section ends with praise of God’s glory. Salvation begins in the Father’s eternal love, is secured by the Son’s life, death and resurrection, and is brought home to us by the Spirit.

Adopted into the family

Paul describes the whole Trinity at work in our adoption: “when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Galatians 4:4–6). The Father sends the Son to redeem slaves, and sends the Spirit to make us cry “Father”. We are no longer slaves but sons, and heirs.

Access to the Father

“For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Ephesians 2:18). Christ preached peace to those far and near, Jews and Gentiles, and now both come to the Father through the Son by the Spirit. Paul goes on to describe the church as a temple built on Christ, “a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22). Christian prayer and worship are Trinitarian by nature: through the Son, by the Spirit, to the Father.

Brought into eternal love

The night before he died, Jesus prayed that his people would be one, as he and the Father are one; that they would be with him to see the glory the Father gave him “in love before the foundation of the world”; and that “the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them” (John 17:24–26). Salvation flows from the eternal love of the Father for the Son in the Spirit — and brings us into it. Jesus even prays that the world may know that the Father “loved them even as you loved me” (John 17:23).

Working inseparably

In every act of God, all three persons act together. Yet each act is especially associated with one person: creation with the Father, redemption with the Son, sanctification with the Spirit. So we must never imagine a kind Son persuading a reluctant Father, or a Spirit acting independently of Christ. The Spirit unites us to the Son, and in the Son we share his relationship with the Father. That is why believers may call God “Father”.

Assurance from all three

A believer struggling with assurance felt that God was distant. Her pastor walked her through Ephesians 1, showing how the Father had chosen her, the Son had redeemed her and the Spirit had sealed her. Her salvation did not rest on her feelings, but on the work of all three persons. She wept with relief. Can you explain your own salvation in terms of what the Father, the Son and the Spirit have each done?

Paul’s own prayer shows the pattern: he bows before the Father, asks that believers be “strengthened with power through his Spirit”, so “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith”, and that they may know “the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” (Ephesians 3:14–19).

For reflection

Read Ephesians 1:3–14: what does each person do in your salvation? How does Galatians 4:4–7 change the way you relate to God? What does it mean to have “access in one Spirit to the Father” through Christ?

6.title: Living with the Triune God
6.essay:
The Trinity is not only to be believed. It is to be lived. The God who is Father, Son and Spirit shapes our prayer, our worship, our relationships and our hope.

Prayer

Jesus taught us to pray, “Our Father in heaven” (Matthew 6:9). We pray in Jesus’ name, trusting in his work (John 14:13). And the Spirit helps us, interceding for us when we do not know what to pray (Romans 8:26). Every Christian prayer is a small sharing in the life of the Trinity. Paul’s great prayer in Ephesians 3 is shaped this way: to the Father, for strength by the Spirit, that Christ may dwell in our hearts, so that we may know the love of Christ and be filled with all the fullness of God (Ephesians 3:14–19).

Worship

Christian worship is Trinitarian. We sing to the Father, praise the Son and pray for the Spirit. Many of the church’s greatest hymns and doxologies give glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit together. In John’s vision of heaven, God sits on the throne, the Lamb who was slain stands before it, and the seven spirits of God — which many take to mean the Holy Spirit — burn before the throne (Revelation 4–5). The Trinity is the centre of heaven’s worship.

And our study should end where Paul’s deepest theology ends: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!… For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever” (Romans 11:33–36). A God we could fully understand would not be God. Mystery should lead us not to frustration but to worship.

Love

“God is love” (1 John 4:8), and this is true because God has always been a fellowship of love. Before creation, the Father loved the Son (John 17:24). God did not need to create in order to have someone to love. Relationship is not an afterthought in reality; persons in loving relationship are at the heart of all that is. That is why loneliness feels so wrong, and why community matters so much for people made in God’s image. Our love for one another reflects the love within God.

Unity in the church

Jesus prayed that his people would be one, “just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you” (John 17:21). The church’s unity is meant to reflect the unity of the Trinity: “there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone” (1 Corinthians 12:4–6). Many members, one body; diverse gifts, one God.

Healthy faith honours all three persons. Some traditions neglect the Spirit; others think of the Spirit only in terms of gifts and forget the Father’s love or the Son’s cross. The Trinity keeps us balanced.

The blessing

Paul ended a letter to a troubled church with words that churches still use: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:14). The triune God is not a doctrine we keep at a distance. He is the God who blesses us.

One Christian woman began ending each day by praying those words over her family — thanking the Father for his love, the Son for his grace and the Spirit for his fellowship. That simple habit changed how she thought about God.

For ever

In the new creation, we will see the glory of God in the face of Christ, filled with the Spirit, for ever. The Trinity will be our eternal joy.

For reflection

How does knowing God as Father, Son and Spirit shape your prayers? What does it mean that God has always been a fellowship of love? Which person of the Trinity do you think about least, and how could you grow in knowing him? Pray 2 Corinthians 13:14 for someone this week.
